summary: This RFC lists currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. It obsoletes RFC 900 and earlier editions. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 943.

eli5.summary: A big table of agreed numbers computers use to name things like services and protocols. A newer table later replaced it.

subtitle: Registry of assigned values for Internet protocols and network addresses

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew, protocols and systems needed to assign unique values for network addresses, protocol types, port numbers and other identifiers. A central registry was needed to prevent conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 923 documents the assigned values for network addresses in Classes A, B, and C; protocol numbers; TCP and UDP port assignments; autonomous system numbers; and ARPANET logical addresses, with responsible parties listed for each.
tldr.outcome: This snapshot of assignments from October 1984 helped coordinate resource allocation across the ARPANET and early Internet. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 943 as assignments continued to evolve.

today: RFC 923 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 943. It is a snapshot of the assigned numbers as of October 1984, early in the ARPANET and Internet era.

sections.title: Network Assignments and Coordination
sections.content: RFC 923 is the official registry of assigned numbers used in Internet protocols as of October 1984. The Internet Protocol (IP) uses 32-bit addresses divided into network and local address portions, with three classes providing different tradeoffs between network size and host capacity. Class A provides 128 networks with 16 million hosts each; Class B provides 16,384 networks with 65,536 hosts each; Class C provides over 2 million networks with 256 hosts each. The RFC lists all assigned network numbers across these classes, including networks for research institutions, defense agencies, government organizations, and commercial entities. Joyce Reynolds at USC-ISI maintained and assigned these numbers in 1984.
sections.eli5: The Internet had networks in three sizes: really big (Class A), medium (Class B), and small (Class C). This list says which big organization got which network number to avoid conflicts.

sections.title: Protocol and Port Assignments
sections.content: IP includes a protocol field to identify the next-level protocol being carried. RFC 923 lists assigned protocol numbers from 0 to 255: 0 is reserved, 1 is ICMP, 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, and many others including GGP, ST, EGP, and various experimental protocols. TCP and UDP use port numbers to name the ends of logical connections. The RFC lists well-known port assignments: port 21 is FTP control, port 23 is Telnet, port 25 is SMTP, port 53 is DNS, port 69 is TFTP, and port 111 is SUN RPC, among many others. These assignments let services be reached at standard contact ports without prior negotiation.
sections.eli5: Protocols are like languages computers use. Port numbers are like mailboxes on a computer. The list says protocol number 6 is TCP, protocol 17 is UDP, and port 25 is always for email.

sections.title: Autonomous System Numbers
sections.content: The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) lets groups of gateways form autonomous systems (AS). Each AS has a 16-bit identifier. RFC 923 assigns autonomous system numbers to early Internet backbone operators and institutions: the BBN gateways (AS 1), various research institutions like ISI (AS 4), CMU (AS 9), and universities like Stanford (AS 32) and RAND (AS 21). The numbers help routing protocols identify administrative boundaries and enable inter-domain routing decisions.
sections.eli5: Big organizations running their own networks got assigned numbers so routing protocols could tell one backbone from another. The BBN got number 1, ISI got number 4.

sections.title: Address Classes and Notation
sections.content: RFC 923 defines dotted decimal notation for IP addresses, dividing the 32-bit address into four 8-bit fields: Class A networks use the first 7 bits (nnn.rrr.rrr.rrr), Class B uses 14 bits (nnn.nnn.rrr.rrr), and Class C uses 21 bits (nnn.nnn.nnn.rrr), where nnn represents network bits and rrr represents local address bits. Special addresses have functional meaning: address 0 means "this network", and all ones means "all hosts". The RFC marks network assignments with codes: R for research, D for defense, G for government, C for commercial. Temporary assignments use a T suffix with a -TEMP suffix on the name during transition periods.
sections.eli5: IP addresses have a special format: four numbers separated by dots. The first number in a Class A address like 10.x.x.x goes in one bin, a Class B like 128.9.x.x in another, and a Class C like 200.1.1.x in a third.

sections.title: ARPANET Logical Addressing
sections.content: RFC 923 also documents ARPANET logical addressing, which provides a facility for naming logical connections independent of the underlying network topology. There are 49,152 possible logical host addresses, with portions reserved for standard uses. This addresses the needs of the ARPANET infrastructure to support virtual circuits and named connections separate from the TCP/IP layer addresses.
sections.eli5: In addition to regular network addresses, ARPANET had a separate system of logical addresses for keeping track of connections without caring about the actual network topology.
